True T-72F Error Code N7 Explanation
On the True T-72F-HC reach-in freezer, the N7 error code is a defrost system fault.  This Freezer uses a Grasslin defrost timer that controls the defrost cycle. The N7 code typically indicates that the defrost timer has detected a fault condition that prevents the normal defrost sequence from completing manual.

What N7 Error Means
Defrost timer fault — the internal timer or its associated relay/contacts are not operating as expected.

This can be caused by:

A failed or loose defrost timer relay

Shorted or open defrost timer contacts

Power supply issues to the timer

Wiring faults in the defrost circuit

Moisture or corrosion in the timer assembly

Reported Issue

WO #355478489 – Grocery / Refrigeration / Frozen Food Case – Low Temperature Rack Leak

Store reported a refrigerant leak on the discharge equalizer line directly below the white water reclaim three-way valve. Previous technician observed oil residue at this location the day prior. Receiver level dropped from approximately 20% to 0%, with fresh oil accumulation beneath the valve assembly, indicating an active refrigerant leak. Rack utilizes R-404A.

Status

Operational – Follow-Up Recommended

Service Performed

Arrived onsite and checked in with Store Manager Andrea. Accessed the low-temperature rack and verified the reported leak location. Performed a leak inspection using a soap bubble solution and confirmed an active leak on the discharge equalizer line below the water reclaim three-way valve.

Pumped the rack down to isolate the affected section and completed the necessary brazing repair. After allowing the repair to cool, pressure integrity was verified and the repaired section was evacuated to below 500 microns, confirming a deep vacuum prior to returning the system to service.

The rack was restarted and the repaired area was leak checked a second time with no additional leaks detected. Charged the system with 72 pounds of R-404A to restore the receiver level to the proper operating range.

Completed all required refrigerant leak documentation and notified store personnel of repairs performed.

Recommendations

Recommend a follow-up visit to verify receiver level remains stable, confirm there is no loss of refrigerant following the repair, and ensure long-term system integrity.

Upon arrival, I checked in with the manager on site. The manager reported that the entire produce wall and multiple refrigerated cases throughout the store had been running warm. However, the case temperatures recovered overnight during the early morning hours.

I gained access to the rack house and inspected the receiver. There was no ball visible in the receiver sight glass, and the liquid line sight glass was flashing, indicating a low refrigerant charge. I performed a leak inspection and located a refrigerant leak at a flare fitting on one of the low-temperature compressors. I tightened the flare nut, which stopped the leak. I then completed a thorough leak search of the remaining rack components, condenser, and accessible piping throughout the store and found no additional leaks.

There was one 100 lb cylinder of R407A available on site, which I added to the system. This was not enough to clear the flashing liquid sight glass or restore the receiver level. Maintenance then delivered two additional 100 lb cylinders of R407A. I added both cylinders to the system until the liquid sight glass cleared and the receiver level indicated a floating ball.

After restoring the refrigerant charge, the produce cooler alarm cleared and all refrigerated cases returned to, or were approaching, their setpoints. System operation was verified, and all equipment was operating normally at the time of departure. This call is complete.
Used 300 lbs of 407a supplied by the customer
No injuries were reported on this job.

Upon arrival, I checked in with the manager on site and located the deli service case reported to be running warm. Both sections of the case had been emptied, although only one section was affected.

I connected gauges to the suction service port and installed a temperature clamp on the suction line. Initial superheat measured approximately 21°F, indicating the TXV was underfeeding the evaporator. I removed the adjustment cap from the TXV and adjusted the valve while lightly tapping the valve body. Superheat decreased to approximately 10°F; however, after monitoring operation, the valve failed to maintain a stable setting. Superheat continually fluctuated between 10°F and 20°F, confirming inconsistent TXV operation.

This case is equipped with the original TXV, and the adjacent case previously required TXV replacement due to the same failure. The TXV on this case has failed and will need to be replaced. Return visit required to replace the TXV and verify proper system operation. This call is incomplete.

Picked up five cylinders of R-404A refrigerant from United Refrigeration prior to arriving on site. Upon arrival, checked in with the manager and proceeded to the rack. Added four cylinders of R-404A to the system until the liquid line sight glass cleared, indicating a solid column of liquid.

After confirming with the manager that approval had been given by Dave to replace the TXV on the deli service case, I pumped down the circuit and recovered the remaining refrigerant from the isolated section into the main suction header. Removed the failed TXV and installed the new valve. Pulled the system into a deep vacuum, then reopened the liquid and suction service valves to return the circuit to operation.

Monitored system operation while the cases pulled down in temperature. Adjusted the new TXV several times to achieve and maintain the proper superheat. Final superheat stabilized at approximately 10°F. Both sections of the deli service case pulled down to 36°F and were operating. However the temperature climbed back up to 39 degrees. The suction pressure was 62 psi on the medium temp and the setpoint is 50 psi. Tried to adjust the EPR but it would not change the suction pressure in the circuit. The discharge was 289 psi. I picked some water hoses and a sprinkler. Hooked up the hose to a water source and put the sprinkler under the condenser and it is now lowering the discharge pressure. This has lowered the suction pressure and the case temp is dropping. This is a temporary fix for the weekend. Call complete

Problem: Pharmacy running warm due to main sales floor RTU #2  being down. Caused by single phasing contactor on compressor 2 and bad motor protector on compressor 1. 
Resolution: Arrived at store and checked in with SM. Checked the pharmacy and the lead pharmacist was not in. There is two digital thermometers on the counter and they were both reading 73°. Checked the BX and RTU 2 was reading an average of 72°. Space temp 1 was 72° and space temp 2 was 69°. The supply temp was 67° and return was 70°. Two stages of cooling were being called for. Checked the unit and found neither compressor running. Compressor 1 was being called for and compressor 2 breaker was tripped. Compressor 1 has parts on order from another dispatch. Began troubleshooting compressor 2. Removed electrical cover from the compressor and noticed L1 was slightly tarnished. And the wire from the terminal to the motor protector was burned. Removed all three legs and ohmed out the compressor across the windings and to ground, found no problems with the compressor. Repaired the damaged wire from L1 to motor protector. Ohmed out compressor and wire on bottom of contactor and it was good. Noticed L1 on the line side of contactor was melted. Removed and cut the damaged wire and tightened all connections. Tested the compressor and found it was single phasing due to L1 on contactor being bad. Took apart contactor to try and clean points but L1 is too damaged. Had a slightly different contactor on my van with an auxiliary. Replaced the damaged contactor with it to get the compressor running. Will need to return with the correct contactor for compressor 2. Right now the supply temp has dropped to 55°. 
Parts Needed:

•	The appliance serviced.
•	The refrigerant type added.
•	Total amount of refrigerant recovered (if any)
•	Total amount of refrigerant added (including adding back recovered refrigerant)
•	Date refrigerant was added. 
•	Leak location(s)

A note on HVAC units:
If refrigerant is required for an HVAC unit with multiple independent circuits/stages, keep in mind that each independent circuit is considered a separate appliance, so refrigerant adds on each circuit must be logged individually.

This requirement applies to ANY store/facility, any refrigerant type, including CO2, and any type of leak repair, including warranty work or any other special project.

Arrived on site. Checked in with Jackie Jimenez. Upon arrival, I made my way to RDM. I found side A in temp but side B not in temp. I confirmed air flow was good and coil wasn’t frozen. I then checked on RDM my transducer and probes. Side A read suction pressure of 3psi. Side B read suction pressure of 65 psi. I made my way to roof and located condensing unit. I checked my suction pressure there and it read 55psi. I then verified transducers and side A read 3 psi and side B read 65psi. I opened cap for side A transducer and it was completely closed. I went ahead and opened it all the way. Now both side A and Side B read 55 psi. Side B is now in temperature. Since side A had valves open at 100 percent because transducer read 3psi, it was causing suction line to read colder than normal causing side B to keep EEVs closed. Since RDM uses probes and transducers to operate, with a closed transducer it will cause suction line to flood back and since Side A and B share suction line, side B would stay close. After opening transducer for side A, side B dropped into temp and stayed in temp. Unit is working properly. Now management stated that at night it’s when side B goes down. Mike Laurel will be converting call to OT approved. Will come back at night to verify case stays running.

Scope of Work:

Provide all labor, equipment, and materials required to replace the failed LG compressor located on a sloped roof.

Work to include:

* Dispatch two refrigeration technicians for one full workday to safely complete the compressor replacement.
* Recover the existing refrigerant charge using EPA-approved recovery equipment.
* Isolate the refrigeration circuit and remove the failed LG compressor.
* Cut out and unbraze the existing compressor from the system.
* Properly dispose of the failed compressor in accordance with applicable environmental regulations.
* Install the new OEM LG compressor.
* Braze all refrigerant connections using proper nitrogen purge procedures to minimize internal oxidation.
* Replace filter-drier(s) as required during compressor replacement.
* Pressure test the repaired system to verify there are no refrigerant leaks.
* Pull an EPA-mandated deep vacuum to industry standards, verifying the system reaches and holds the required micron level before charging.
* Recharge the system with new (virgin) refrigerant to the manufacturer’s specified charge.
* Start and commission the equipment.
* Verify proper compressor rotation (if applicable), operating pressures, superheat, subcooling, compressor amperage, and overall system performance.
* Confirm the unit is operating within manufacturer specifications before returning it to service.
* Clean the work area and remove all replaced materials from the site.

 Issue: Starbucks reach in case is too warm.


Resolution: Upon arrival, found the unit inoperative with no cooling. 


Performed electrical diagnostics and verified proper line voltage was present to the controller. Troubleshot the control circuit and determined the main power switch had failed, preventing power from reaching the controller and refrigeration system.

Upon arrival, I checked in with Salesforce and management. An emergency call was made regarding the high temperature in the produce walk-in cooler. 

I located the asset and noticed that all the fan motors were off. I began verifying the main power switch and traced it all the way to the raceway where the fan motors were plugged in. I was getting 120 volts, but the fans were still not turning on. I located WICP-7 and found the controller for the produce walk-in cooler. I discovered that the contactor was energized, and both the incoming and outgoing voltages were correct. I also verified that I was getting coil voltage. While I was examining the contactor for the fans, I noticed a burnt smell. I found that the defrost contactor had melted at the bottom. I replaced the contactor with a new one that had the same specifications as the one that was faulty.

I then went down to the walk-in and removed the fan guard. I tried spinning the blade, but the motors were seized. I went to my van and found four new universal motors. I had to wire each one individually to install the motors. I began putting back the fan blades and guards, cleaned up the work area, and watched the temperature drop to the RDM set-point. I wrote my notes and checked out with management.

notes.text: Tech was NOT onsite for another call.

*Rack B high temps 

Arrived on site and located rack, sight glass was flashing, receiver was empty, suction pressure was high, discharge pressure was high. 

Found compressor 2 Valved off, it’s bad. Compressor 4 toggle switch was off, turned on. 

Went to roof and there is one bad motor, already written up. Condenser is clean. 

Went down and found my liquid line was over 100°, made sure split valve wasn’t energized, ended up finding a discharge line in the ceiling above the rack was shut off, opened it up and brought the discharge pressure down from 290 to 238. 

I fixed a couple small leaks on rack, added 50lbs. Found sight glass still flashing, took pressure drop across cores and found 11 psi drop. Pumped rack down and changed core driers. Turned rack back on 

Cases are slowly dropping but need to get compressor 2 changed out. Made sure nothing was dumping into the suction to elevate suction pressure. Due to there being such a high load on the rack from all the issues it will take some time to recover. 

Also found rack suction setpoint was set to 25psi, this is incorrect as the rack calls for a +16° SST, converted to 407a pressure and set rack suction pressure for 37.8psi.

Also found several setpoints way too low, I found a beer case set at 28°, went through and slightly adjusted setpoints as this would help in the meantime of a compressor being down. 

I believe several sorits are out of adjustment, too much oil in the system etc

Was gonna throw a sprinkler on the condenser but there is no spigot on the outside of the building and can’t leave doors open overnight. 

Let Kent know of the issues and we will see how rack does overnight, no cases in alarm at this point but some are still elevated but below alarm setpoint. 

Leaving in follow up for now until we confirm everything is good

6/30/2026
Upon arrival, checked in with the store manager. She let me know which circuit was running too cold. So I then headed over to the MDU, checked for airflow. There was no airflow. Product was still loaded. I had the manager to remove the product. While the manager was removing the product, I headed over to the back area to the E2 controller to check the MDU operations on the rack. The MDU had four circuits. Three circuits was running under set point, while one of the circuit was running well above set point in alarm. So then I headed over to, once the product was pulled, I removed the bottom deck pans from the MDU, and I noticed there was a case full of water, backed up, drains was clogged, coils was iced up, line sets was iced up, and there was water underneath the fans. Fans was hitting the water. So due to the one circuit running warm above set point, the compressor was never cutting off, continuously running, freezing up the coils, causing the other three cases to run cold, while the one circuit running hot. So then I vacuumed all the water out of the MDU, cleared the drains, cleared the buffer box underneath the case. Then got water pouring down the drain, made sure it was draining, and the activator was reacting to the pressure out the buffer box, removing the water from the buffer box, which it was. Then I focused on getting the ice off the line set in the back of the coil. Once I got the ice off, I cut back on refrigeration, plugged back in my fans. Then I checked for airflow. Airflow was restored. Put the bottom deck pans back on, headed to the E2 controller to check the temperature of the cases. All cases was now running normally. The one case was out of alarm, and the circuit is now running at set point. I let the manager know of my findings. No further issues with this call. Call complete.
No injuries were reported on this job.

As of July 10, 2023, technicians no longer have to call (or text) the H-E-B refrigerant hotline to get approval to add refrigerant. 

Instead, technicians and/or vendor recordkeepers MUST create a “call log” in MyFacility within 72 hours of the refrigerant add, documenting: 
•	The appliance serviced.
•	The refrigerant type added.
•	Total amount of refrigerant recovered (if any)
•	Total amount of refrigerant added (including adding back recovered refrigerant)
•	Date refrigerant was added. 
•	Leak location(s) 

There will be an additional optional free text space for other notes.  

**PLEASE copy and paste the following link to access the HEB COMPRESSOR REPLACEMENT FORM:

https://url.us.m.mimecastprotect.com/s/OVkRCQWRVRFxmxD1SxfnTGgCW1?domain=app.smartsheet.com

Technicians and/or vendor record keepers MUST record refrigerant adds on the following appliance types:
•	Any refrigeration appliance except for self-contains (e.g., bottle coolers on the store floor), regardless of charge size.
•	Any HVAC appliance, regardless of charge size
A note on HVAC units:
If refrigerant is required for an HVAC unit with multiple independent circuits/stages, keep in mind that each independent circuit is considered a separate appliance, so refrigerant adds on each circuit must be logged individually.
?	Example: if tech is working on PACU2, an HVAC unit with 4 separate circuits/stages, and wants to add gas to circuit 1 (PACU2a) and circuit 3 (PACU2c), tech or recordkeeper must enter a separate call log for PACU2a and PACU2c with the amount of refrigerant added.

Call logs are required to be entered in MyFacility within 72 hours of the refrigerant add. Found several medium-temperature cases rising above 50°F during defrost, with some reaching as high as 55°F. Updated defrost schedules to factory-recommended settings and changed the termination method on multiple circuits from time termination to case temperature termination so defrost cycles end at the proper case temperature. Collected case information and will provide a quote to install the divider. Also found all medium-temperature walk-in evaporator coils heavily soiled, reducing efficiency, and recommend cleaning the coils. Will return to fine-tune the expansion valves to better balance case temperatures. Recommended keeping the door closed so both refrigeration circuits can operate as designed.

Equipment: Mobile Merchandise Produce Case (Closest to Store Entrance)

Responded to a complaint of the mobile merchandise produce case running warm.

Upon arrival, observed multiple boxes stacked directly against the condenser air intake, severely restricting airflow. Proper condenser airflow is critical for heat rejection, and the obstruction was creating conditions that could cause the unit to trip on high-head pressure. The boxes will need to be removed or stored on a raised platform to maintain adequate airflow to the condenser.

Store personnel advised that they routinely unplug and reconnect the unit whenever it shuts off. During inspection, found the condenser air filter heavily contaminated with debris. Removed the filter, cleaned it thoroughly, and reinstalled it. Inspected the condenser coil and found it clean with no debris or damage requiring additional cleaning.

Monitored the unit throughout the service visit and observed normal refrigeration operation. The compressor and condenser cycled normally during the entire time on-site, and no faults occurred while the unit had adequate airflow.

Based on the inspection and operating conditions, the most likely cause of the intermittent warming is high-head pressure caused by restricted condenser airflow from the blocked air intake, compounded by the high ambient temperature in the area. The dirty condenser filter also contributed to reduced airflow.

Result: Cleaned the condenser air filter and verified normal unit operation. Advised store personnel that the area around the condenser intake must remain clear of boxes to provide adequate airflow and prevent future high-head pressure trips and warming issues.
No injuries were reported on this job.

6/30 Tyler- Arrived on site and checked in with Jim and Bruce. Coordinated a production shutdown to allow repairs, then entered the box and performed a leak check. Located a major refrigerant leak on Evaporator 1. After receiving approval from Bruce, isolated the circuit, pumped the zone down, and repaired two leaks: a small rub-through on the suction header caused by a capillary tube and a large pinhole at the outlet of the distributor where the distributor tube enters the coil. Brazed both leaks, pressure tested the circuit, and verified the repairs using an electronic leak detector and bubble solution with no additional leaks found.

Also found Compressor 6 tripped on oil safety, which was causing high suction pressure on Suction Group 2 and contributing to elevated water chiller temperatures. Additionally, found the water chiller was not distributing water evenly across the evaporator. The flow requires adjustment by the plumbing contractor, and Dan has been notified of the issue. Assisted Jim with removing the tanks from the previous night's work while on site.

Intermittently found a temperature sensor fault on Circuit 1B. To maintain refrigeration, overrode the circuit temperature to **38°F** until repairs can be completed. The system will require a return visit to verify the refrigerant charge, add additional refrigerant (approximately a couple hundred pounds), and replace the faulty 1B temperature sensor. After removing all the electrical covers, I connected the old condensate pump’s safety circuit wires to the Mitsubishi mini split, which sends a signal to the thermostat when the pump fails. Unfortunately, the float switch was faulty. I removed the old pump and float switch, then installed the new condensate pump and float switch, which required different wiring. After completing the installation, I returned to the roof to restore power. Upon coming back downstairs, the thermostat displayed “wait.” I waited for 10 minutes, but the message remained unchanged. I discovered it was awaiting a signal, and the condensation pump was flashing green. I realized the wiring was incorrect, so I went back upstairs to disconnect the power, returned downstairs to rewire it properly, and then reconnected the power on the roof. After five minutes, the thermostat began displaying temperature readings, and the light on the condensate pump remained green. I tested the pump by pouring water into it, and it functioned without leaks, with the thermostat operating correctly.

On both units all 4 compressors were running as well as the condensing fans.  Both units' supply fans were running, and both desiccant wheels were spinning.  There was a lot of ice on the coils and metering devices for both units though so we may need to de-ice those and then troubleshoot the cooling circuits.

7/1/26 Jess- I arrived and checked in using the corrigo app. I then spoke to Thomas upon entering the building. I went up to RTU# 1&2. There was no ice on the coils, fans were working, and compressor were on. Coils look to have been recently cleaned. I went down to the E3 and both units were at setpoint of 70 degrees. The store humidity was 50%. I graphed the temps and humidity levels and they both have seem to drop drastically since the ice was removed. I noticed RTU#2 supply temp reading was high. I went up to the unit and tried to locate the temp sensor to test. I  found the temp sensor located in the duct drop on the sales floor. I will return tomorrow morning to use the store lift to test.
No injuries were reported on this job.
Tech was NOT onsite for another call.
JESS IS IN CORRIGO

7/2/26 Jess- I arrived on-site and checked in using the corrigo app. I then gained access to the building and checked in with Sara. I grabbed the wave lift and test the supply air sensor fpr Rtu #2 with ice water. It is reading 32.5 degree in the ice water. I then went up to the unit and started troubleshooting. I took pressure readings on all 4 circuirts and superheat. I had high superheat and low suction on circuit B. I took delta T across evap coil at had 22 degrees. I checked the liquid drier temp and had same temp reading on both sides for B. I took temps across the react wheel, supply cabinet and process cabinet. My hot gas dump valve was feeding on circuit B because of low suction adding superheat to the circuit. I added 6lbs of R410 from my truck stock. I leak checked the unit and found the danfoss high pressure safety on circuit B was leaking from Cap-tube service port connection. I tightened it down and the leak stopped. I now have 18 degrees superheat at the compressors per Munters spec. My supply temp sensor is reading high because the unit is running in dehumifaction mode because the store dew point 50% is above E3 setpoint of 45%. I took subcooling on cirucit B and had 8 degrees. I cleaned condensate traps on both RTU# 1&2. I found A06 ice cream freezer doors in alarm and had poor air flow on T1 & T2, I forced a defrost and checked back. Alarms cleared and temps came down. The doors have a lot of moisture build up in them. I spoke to Sara and said she may want to put a ticket in for this circuit or have employee wipe them out during next defrost. This job is complete
No injuries were reported on this job.

Took a look at wiring diagram and controller just to double check staging of compressor is working correctly. Found that the micro thermo sensor is only for monitoring and doesn’t control the unit. The sensor that controls the unit is close towards the front of the door on the return side. The micro thermo is towards the back on the supply side of the coil. Due to door being open the sensor that controls the unit was reading high temp causing unit to run longer. Therefore the microthermo sensor of the supply side was reading lower temp due to unit running longer than needed to reach set point. Still double checked to make sure it was reading correctly. Manager had said a piece of paper or cardboard had fallen into the sliding rail for the door. They took it out and door was able to shut again. Verified compressor, condenser fan motor, evaporator fan motor, and refrigeration system operation.

Checked the liquid line filter drier and found a measurable temperature drop across the drier, indicating a restriction.

Verified the liquid line solenoid valve was energized and operating correctly.

Performed extensive troubleshooting of the Dixell controller, case temperature sensor, E2 monitoring circuit, and associated wiring.

Installed a replacement temperature sensor for testing; however, the replacement sensor on hand was not the correct sensor for this application and caused the controller to display a P1 DEF alarm. Reinstalled the original sensor, restoring normal controller operation.

Verified the Dixell controller accurately reads and controls the case temperature. Continued troubleshooting determined the refrigeration system is operating, but the E2 monitoring circuit is receiving an incorrect temperature reading. Based on testing, the E2 temperature sensor has failed.

Placing the call in follow-up to return with the correct E2 temperature sensor and replace the restricted liquid line filter drier. Both repairs are required to restore proper E2 temperature reporting and eliminate the liquid line restriction.

Checked in with Jose upon arrival. Call was for A15 T2 running warm. A separate call for A15 T1 was booked and handled by Dalton .

Upon inspection, the case was in defrost. Temperatures remained elevated around 4:30 PM. Store personnel were directed to pull product from the bottom shelves. After defrost completed and all fans were confirmed running, the plenum was lifted, revealing a thick wall of heavy frost in the middle of the coil blocking airflow. No ice was present. The case had been deiced earlier that morning and TXV screens had been cleaned at that time.

A hot water bucket and pump were used to melt the frost. A clogged drain was found and cleared. The circuit was then pumped down and all refrigerant was recovered to inspect the TXV. The valve was heavily fouled and the needle could not be removed for cleaning and oiling, necessitating a full valve replacement.

The old valve was unsweated and replaced with a new SBQE body, yellow cartridge, and KT-43-VZ power head. A vacuum was pulled below 500 microns, then broken with suction pressure. Leak check was performed with no leaks found. The liquid line was opened and the case was allowed to pull down to temperature. Case was nearing setpoint with superheat confirmed at 3-5°F.

It was also noted that customer traffic was exceptionally high due to a 50% off ice cream sale, with customers observed holding case doors open for extended periods, contributing to the case load.

Materials were cleaned up and a check-out was completed with store personnel.

Equipment: Walk-In Meat Freezer F01

Responded to a service call for a water leak from the drain pan of the walk-in meat freezer.

Upon arrival, inspected the evaporator section and found the drain pan filled with ice. The drain heater was cold to the touch, preventing the drain from staying clear and allowing ice to accumulate in the drain pan, which resulted in the reported water leak.

Accessed the top of the freezer and verified that power was present at the drain heater circuit. After consulting with store maintenance, learned that the drain heater is supplied through a GFCI receptacle located in the neighboring fruit cooler. Inspected the GFCI and found it tripped. Reset the GFCI, restoring power to the drain heater. Confirmed proper operation by verifying that the heater became warm shortly after power was restored.

Allowed the drain heater sufficient time to melt the ice within the drain line. Removed the drain pan and completely deiced and cleaned it before reinstalling it. Once the drain system was clear, reassembled the evaporator section, restored the refrigerant valve to the operating position, restarted the evaporator fans, and returned the freezer to service.

Monitored the freezer during operation and verified proper drain heater operation, unrestricted drainage, and normal refrigeration performance. Observed the freezer pulling down to its normal operating temperature.

Result: Reset the tripped GFCI supplying the drain heater, restoring heater operation. Deiced the drain pan and drain system, reassembled the unit, and confirmed the freezer was operating normally with proper drainage and no further water leakage at the time of departure.

Arrived on site and checked in with the MIC. After checking in, I had the MIC remove all product from the affected case so repairs could be performed. Once the product was removed, I disassembled the case and inspected the evaporator coil. Upon inspection, I found the evaporator coil completely iced over, restricting airflow through the case.

I thoroughly deiced the evaporator coil and then connected my gauges and a temperature clamp to evaluate system operation and obtain a superheat reading. Initially, the superheat reading was within an acceptable range. However, after allowing the case to run for a period of time, the superheat steadily dropped into the negative range, indicating that the electronic expansion valve was overfeeding the evaporator and flooding the coil with refrigerant. This condition is what caused the evaporator to repeatedly ice over.

To further diagnose the issue, I reviewed the supporting documentation and input list for the RDM controller. I verified that Input 4 is assigned to the suction line temperature probe. I compared the temperature reported by the controller to my calibrated temperature clamp and found a significant discrepancy. The RDM controller was reading the suction line temperature at 25°F, while my temperature clamp measured 15°F. This inaccurate temperature reading is causing the controller to incorrectly regulate the electronic expansion valve, resulting in the valve overfeeding the evaporator.

Based on these findings, the suction line temperature probe has been identified as the likely cause of the issue. A technician will return tomorrow to replace the suction line temperature probe and verify proper valve operation, superheat, and overall case performance.

After completing diagnostics, I reassembled the case, cleaned the work area, and checked out with the MIC.

I think it would be good to ask the electric company to raise the tap at the transformer output so that it delivers the correct voltage (at least 208 volts). By design, these compressors should never operate at this voltage (just a personal opinion).

The minimum operating voltage for these compressors at a frequency of 60 Hz is 208 volts. They operate below 200 volts most of the time. In the afternoon, the voltage at this rack approaches 190 volts (almost 10% below the compressor's minimum operating voltage). On the other hand, the voltage of the relay coil for the phase monitor is 240 volts (almost 20% higher than the rack voltage in the afternoons). When the compressors start, this voltage drops even further and is very likely insufficient to keep the relay coil energized, even if the phase monitor is "green."

Arrived on site and checked in with manager Anthony, who directed me to the walk-in produce cooler. Upon initial inspection, I observed the evaporator fan blades making contact with standing water in the drain pan. Water was also present on the floor, and heavy ice buildup was found on both the front and rear of the evaporator coil.

Placed the system into emergency defrost to begin thawing the ice. After the drain pan thawed, the water still would not drain, indicating a clogged drain line. Used a shop vacuum to clear the drain and then blew the drain line out with nitrogen. Verified that water was flowing properly.

Continued the de-icing process using hot water until the evaporator coil was completely free of ice. Once the coil was fully thawed, vacuumed and blew out the drain line a second time to ensure it was completely clear and confirmed proper drainage. Checked the defrost heaters and verified they were operating correctly. Determined the ice buildup was caused by the backed-up drain line, not a defrost heater failure.

Monitored the walk-in cooler through its refrigeration cycle until it reached the set point and confirmed normal operation.

If the work is out of contract, a quote is required and must go through the approval process.
   •   Save Mart is temporarily prioritizing only emergency and life safety-related repairs. Quotes that do not get approved will be placed on hold.
   •   If you need help determining whether a repair qualifies as an emergency or life safety issue, please reach out to your Service Manager.
****Anyone adding refrigerant over 50# to a Save Mart/Food Maxx/Lucky supermarket needs to be emailing savemart@climatepros.com and your service manager, with the dispatch number, amount of refrigerant that was added, type of gas, where was the leak and if it is repaired. The Save Mart Account Team needs the heads up to notify Save Mart. This needs to come from the technician in the field that is adding the refrigerant.****
****Checking in/out and pausing process for Save mart in the Corrigo app.****
SECOND TECH MUST LEAVE A NOTE WITH TIME AND DATE IN CORRIGO.
•	 When tech gets onsite, please check in Corrigo and manager.
•	If tech needs to place work order in follow up, needs parts etc... Tech is to place the work order on pause with a note. “Need to order parts” Or “Needs to quote repairs” as well as the visible to customer note tech would add to FJX.
•	Select ALL on the drop-down menu.
•	When tech is 100% complete with the work order we can then select the “check out” option. 
•	Once the tech selects “check out” a box will populate with “Work done description” and “Repair category”. In the work done description techs need to put in notes of the work done like they would do their FJX notes stating “call complete”
•	Final step is to fill out the fields asking to enter “Model number” “Serial number” and “LBS lost”
Water One 227214 PO 2908899 FM 416 July 2026

Began inspecting all wiring was not able to find a short or burnt wire anywhere.  Went inside walk-in open up junction boxes expected an electrical and no visible shorts or burnt wires. Remove panels off evaporator inspected solenoid wiring, and was in good condition not rubbing against anything.  Removed wires from control breaker and check them to ground and they were not grounded. Forced freezer to defrost a few times allowed freezer to terminate on its own and Refrigeration turned back on and breaker did not trip.

Restored power and took an amp draw and amps were very low. Upon arrival, checked in with the store manager regarding the meat freezer running warm. I then proceeded to the meat freezer to investigate.

Upon inspection, I found no airflow from the case. There was heavy ice buildup across the entire evaporator coil, including behind the fans, in front of the coil, and on top of the coil.

I shut off refrigeration and power to the unit, then headed to the roof to check rack operations. Logged the freezer in the system and found the case had not been maintaining setpoint for the past three days (since the 24th).

I initiated an emergency defrost and checked rack operation while monitoring DDR differential pressure. DDR differential was reading approximately 6 PSI upon arrival. Adjusted DDR to 16–17 PSI.

I then returned to the van to retrieve my de-icing kit and proceeded to fully de-ice the evaporator coil and surrounding ice buildup. After de-icing, I inspected the screen and found it clean with no restrictions. Checked the case temperature probe and verified it was reading properly.

Once repairs were completed, I reassembled the fan section and restored power and refrigeration to the case.

I returned to the motor room to continue troubleshooting. Checked across the filter driers and found no significant pressure drop. Checked the suction transducer and found it reading approximately 2 degrees off.

I contacted Justin to review findings. Based on discussion, he advised the issue may be related to the power head and that pin adjustments may be needed.

I updated the store manager on findings and explained additional troubleshooting may be required. The manager informed me the store was closing and I would need to leave the site. I advised that the case required further investigation and should not be left without follow-up. Due to store closure, I documented all findings, obtained signature, and left site.

Call placed in follow-up for additional diagnosis and repair.

Systems 1-9 and 1-12 were found in high temperature alarm. Upon inspection of the machine room, six additional systems were also found in alarm. The refrigerant sight glass was bubbling, and the liquid level was at 0.3%. A leak inspection was performed, and five refrigerant leaks were found: four leaks at the hot gas line ball valves for systems 148, 151, 115, and 123, and one smaller leak at the oil separator flange gasket, with a maximum leak detector reading of approximately 1,100 PPM.

Resolution:
The Manager On Call, Justin, was contacted and authorized the repair of the four leaking ball valves. The oil separator flange gasket replacement was deferred until Monday. The authorized leaks were repaired, and the rack was initially charged with 144 lbs of R404A; however, this was not enough to clear the sight glass or fully recover all systems. An additional 96 lbs of R404A were added, bringing the total charge to 240 lbs. After charging, the sight glass became completely clear, all affected systems returned to their set points, and the liquid level stabilized at 26.90%.

3rd Party Check Out: The manager was informed of the repairs performed, the remaining leak at the oil separator flange gasket, and that the rack was left operating properly.

As of July 10, 2023, technicians no longer have to call (or text) the H-E-B refrigerant hotline to get approval to add refrigerant.

Technicians and/or vendor record keepers MUST record refrigerant adds on the following appliance types:
•	Any refrigeration appliance except for self-contains (e.g., bottle coolers on the store floor), regardless of charge size.
•	Any HVAC appliance, regardless of charge size
A note on HVAC units:
If refrigerant is required for an HVAC unit with multiple independent circuits/stages, keep in mind that each independent circuit is considered a separate appliance, so refrigerant adds on each circuit must be logged individually.
?	Example: if tech is working on PACU2, an HVAC unit with 4 separate circuits/stages, and wants to add gas to circuit 1 (PACU2a) and circuit 3 (PACU2c), tech or recordkeeper must enter a separate call log for PACU2a and PACU2c with the amount of refrigerant added.

Call logs are required to be entered in MyFacility within 72 hours of the refrigerant add. Failing to create a call log to record the refrigerant add within 72 hours is the equivalent of not getting approval to add the refrigerant. H-E-B will not pay for any refrigerant add that is not documented within the 72 hour window.

This requirement applies to ANY store/facility, any refrigerant type, including CO2, and any type of leak repair, including warranty work or any other special project.

notes.text: 06.12.26  HVAC & REFER SERVICE

As of July 10, 2023, technicians no longer have to call (or text) the H-E-B refrigerant hotline to get approval to add refrigerant. 

Instead, technicians and/or vendor recordkeepers MUST create a “call log” in MyFacility within 72 hours of the refrigerant add, documenting: 
•	The appliance serviced.
•	The refrigerant type added.
•	Total amount of refrigerant recovered (if any)
•	Total amount of refrigerant added (including adding back recovered refrigerant)
•	Date refrigerant was added.

6/26 System 23C juice case running too cold. All sections were getting down to 25°, except for the center section which had no airflow was at 60°. Removed product from shelf and found that fan motor has failed. Replaced fan motor. Ran system through multiple defrost to get frost buildup off of coil. This section that had the failed fan motor, is where the thermostat bulb is located. The section being warm is what was causing the case to get too cold. System is now maintaining a 34° point.

Upon arrival, checked in with the store manager. Manager identified the case with no airflow and running warm. Headed to the case to investigate. Product was still loaded, so I had the manager remove all product for access. Once product was removed, I removed the bottom deck pans and found the evaporator coil completely iced over, including heavy ice buildup behind and along both sides of the coil, restricting airflow and causing the case to run warm.

I then headed upstairs to the Emerson E2 to check rack operations and review case conditions. While checking the system, I noticed the adjacent case was also running warm. Returned downstairs and verified the neighboring case also had no airflow. Advised the manager to submit an additional work order for that case while on site.

Began de-icing the original case by removing the fan panel to gain access behind the coil. Thoroughly de-iced the entire evaporator coil, including both sides and rear of coil, until all ice buildup was removed. After de-icing, returned upstairs for further troubleshooting. Checked pressure drop across the filter drier and found no significant restriction. Verified rack operation and checked DDR while one case was in defrost; DDR was approximately 16, within normal operating range. Rack charge level was normal and system was not low on refrigerant.

Returned to the case for final inspection and found multiple door gaskets not sealing properly, with sections hanging open and allowing warm, humid air infiltration into the case. This excessive humidity caused heavy frost and ice accumulation on the evaporator coil, leading to airflow restriction and high case temperature.

Informed the manager of findings and recommended gasket replacement/repair to prevent recurring freeze-up issues. Case restored to normal operation at this time. No further issues with this call. Call complete.

Removed the filter assembly, carefully trimmed the restricted section of the hose barb, and reshaped the opening to restore proper airflow. Reassembled the filter assembly and reconnected all vacuum hoses. Manually staged Pump #1 several times and verified the restriction had been eliminated and the shrieking noise was no longer present.

Instead, technicians and/or vendor recordkeepers MUST create a “call log” in MyFacility within 72 hours of the refrigerant add, documenting: 
•	The appliance serviced.
•	The refrigerant type added.
•	Total amount of refrigerant recovered (if any)
•	Total amount of refrigerant added (including adding back recovered refrigerant)
•	Date refrigerant was added. 
•	Leak location(s) 

There will be an additional optional free text space for other notes.  

**PLEASE copy and paste the following link to access the HEB COMPRESSOR REPLACEMENT FORM:

https://url.us.m.mimecastprotect.com/s/OVkRCQWRVRFxmxD1SxfnTGgCW1?domain=app.smartsheet.com

Technicians and/or vendor record keepers MUST record refrigerant adds on the following appliance types:
•	Any refrigeration appliance except for self-contains (e.g., bottle coolers on the store floor), regardless of charge size.
•	Any HVAC appliance, regardless of charge size
A note on HVAC units:
If refrigerant is required for an HVAC unit with multiple independent circuits/stages, keep in mind that each independent circuit is considered a separate appliance, so refrigerant adds on each circuit must be logged individually.
?	Example: if tech is working on PACU2, an HVAC unit with 4 separate circuits/stages, and wants to add gas to circuit 1 (PACU2a) and circuit 3 (PACU2c), tech or recordkeeper must enter a separate call log for PACU2a and PACU2c with the amount of refrigerant added.

Call logs are required to be entered in MyFacility within 72 hours of the refrigerant add. Failing to create a call log to record the refrigerant add within 72 hours is the equivalent of not getting approval to add the refrigerant. H-E-B will not pay for any refrigerant add that is not documented within the 72 hour window.

This requirement applies to ANY store/facility, any refrigerant type, including CO2, and any type of leak repair, including warranty work or any other special project.

checked history

Checked in on sales force and with mic upon arrival. Located reach in freezer to be worked on and found ice buildup up on the left shelf de back wall. Checked doors and found that the left side door does not close properly. Adjusted torque master and verified that door is closing properly. Had product removed from bottom shelves. Found ice buildup up in fan plenum,eev and coil. Shut off liquid line valve and ran water hose and removed all ice from reach in freezer. Opened liquid line valve and verified that freezer is dropping in temperature. Put into defrost and verified that both front and rear defrost heaters are working. Let defrost run its course and verified that case is pulling down in temperature. Case now below alarm set point and  dropping. All is well at this time closing call out complete.
No injuries were reported on this job.
Tech was NOT onsite for another call.
